content.overview: Irrigation faults can originate from filtration, pressure regulation, valves, line damage, emitter blockage, source-water solids or maintenance conditions. Spatial evidence helps distinguish localized from system-wide causes.

vocabulary.definition: A problem affecting one emitter, branch, line or limited area.
A problem affecting much or all of one controlled irrigation zone.
Restriction of water passage caused by physical, chemical or biological material.

sections.title: Use spatial pattern to narrow the fault
sections.body: One low emitter under stable pressure points toward a local restriction; many low emitters after a filter differential change suggest a different fault class.

sections.title: Water chemistry can influence maintenance burden
sections.body: Source-water minerals or other constituents can contribute to deposits or system-management needs, but the exact mechanism should be verified rather than assumed from EC alone.

sections.title: Root-zone consequences strengthen the diagnosis
sections.body: Low output followed by faster dryback or localized EC rise creates a stronger causal chain than flow data alone.

workedExamples: A partially clogged filter reduces output across one zone and root-zone EC rises in the same area; investigate delivery-driven concentration before changing the nutrient recipe.
commonMistakes: Blaming the recipe before checking delivery.
Treating every low-output point as a facility-wide pressure problem.
content.practicalApplication: Classify five irrigation fault scenarios as local, zone-level, source/pressure, filtration or unresolved and state the next discriminating measurement.
content.summary: Fault isolation works best when flow, pressure, filtration history and root-zone response converge on the same explanation.
